# Global cursor rules for script issues

_**User**_

create and install a global-level cursor rules file that tells cursor to avoid using exclamation points in shell scripts because it causes the shell to hang waiting on user input for closing "dquote" shell prompts, which is extremely disruptive and problematic. and do a search on github for cursor rule files that cover dquote and other similar basic problematic issues to avoid in shell prompts or when cursor invokes a shell or python script, for example when installing python packages with pip never use the break system packages option, but instead use a `venv` or `uv` instead of trying to install at the system level

---

_**Agent**_

Researching cursor rules structure and searching GitHub for examples covering shell script issues, then drafting a plan for a global rules file.

---

{"references":[{"title":"Web Search Results","chunk":"Here’s what I found about the behavior involving exclamation points (`!`) inside double-quoted strings, the `dquote>` prompt, shell / zsh history expansion, and related “cursor rules” or GitHub threads:\n\n---\n\n### What causes `dquote>` when using `!\"` in zsh\n\n- In **zsh**, `!\"` (an exclamation mark immediately followed by a double quote) triggers history expansion. The shell treats `!\"` as a special sequence: it briefly disables history expansion and then removes the `!\"` from the input, which leaves an unclosed double-quote. That causes the shell to print the `dquote>` continuation prompt, because it thinks the opening `\"` hasn’t been matched. ([unix.stackexchange.com](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/497328/zsh-thinks-unterminated-quote-if-preceded-by-exclamation-mark?utm_source=openai))\n\n- This behavior is *by design* in zsh. To use `!` inside double quotes without this effect, you either need to escape the `!` or disable history expansion. ([bugs-devel.debian.org](https://bugs-devel.debian.org/1022758?utm_source=openai))\n\n---\n\n### How to avoid or fix the issue\n\nHere are a few options:\n\n1. **Escape the exclamation point**  \n   Inside double quotes: `echo \"foo\\!\"` — the backslash protects the `!`. ([unix.stackexchange.com](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/497328/zsh-thinks-unterminated-quote-if-preceded-by-exclamation-mark?utm_source=openai))\n\n2. **Use single quotes**  \n   Single-quote strings do not trigger history expansion in zsh. Example: `echo 'foo!'`. ([unix.stackexchange.com](https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/497328/zsh-thinks-unterminated-quote-if-preceded-by-exclamation-mark?utm_source=openai))\n\n3. **Disable history expansion entirely**  \n   In zsh, you can do this via `set +H` or `unsetopt hist_expand` (depending on version) in your shell startup (e.g. `~/.zshrc`). Then `!\"` won't trigger that behavior. ([bugs-devel.debian.org](https://bugs-devel.debian.org/1022758?utm_source=openai))\n\n---\n\n### What is “cursor rules file” and how this relates\n\nYou mentioned “cursor rules file shell script exclamation point dquote github”. I found this GitHub issue:\n\n- In **ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh** Issue #7557, someone reported exactly `dquote>` when running something like `echo --message=\"foo!\"`. The description matches: zsh thinks there’s an unterminated quote because of the `!\"`. ([github.com](https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/issues/7557?utm_source=openai))\n\nSo your phrase is referencing that issue: the `dquote>` prompt appears because the `!\"` is misinterpreted by zsh’s history expansion. The “cursor rules file” part may relate to how Cursor IDE or other tools interpret rules or scripts, but that GitHub issue is purely zsh behavior. ([github.com](https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/issues/7557?utm_source=openai))\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can help you craft a shell script or Cursor rule file that avoids this issue cleanly (for zsh, bash, etc.). {"references":[{"title":"Web Search Results","chunk":"Here are some guidelines and example rules (\"cursor rules\") for using **uv**, **pip**, and **virtual environments** properly in a GitHub-based Python project—especially to avoid accidentally installing into system packages or mixing tools. You can adapt these into `.cursor/rules` files or similar for your repo.\n\n---\n\n## Key Concepts\n\n- **uv**: A tool for managing Python environments, dependencies, locking, etc. It favors virtual environments by default and discourages global/system installs. ([gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com/caoer/5b9bbd0fd9fb1dd20d6812b02cfdc3b7?utm_source=openai))  \n- **pip**: The standard installer; when used, ensure it’s invoked in the correct environment or via `uv pip` to stay within isolation. ([gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com/caoer/5b9bbd0fd9fb1dd20d6812b02cfdc3b7?utm_source=openai))  \n- **Virtual environments (venv)**: Isolate project dependencies from the system Python to avoid conflicts. uv’s `venv` commands help manage this. ([gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com/caoer/5b9bbd0fd9fb1dd20d6812b02cfdc3b7?utm_source=openai))  \n\n---\n\n## Suggested Rules File (Cursor Rules)\n\nHere’s a skeleton of rules you might put in a `.cursor/rules/python_uv.toml` or `.cursor/rules/github-actions-uv.mdc` (naming up to your convention).\n\n```yaml\n# .cursor/rules/python_uv.toml or .mdc\n\n---\nalwaysApply: true\n---\n\n# 🐍 Python / Dependency Management Rules\n\n1. Use `uv` exclusively for creating environments & managing dependencies.\n   - Only use `uv venv` (or `uv venv .venv`) to set up virtual environments.\n   - Do *not* run `pip install ...` outside of `uv pip ...` commands.  \n     Reason: uv’s pip interface ensures installation goes to the right virtual environment. ([gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com/caoer/5b9bbd0fd9fb1dd20d6812b02cfdc3b7?utm_source=openai))\n\n2. Avoid system-level installations.\n   - Do *not* use `--user` or install without virtual environment activation.\n   - If needing system install, require an explicit flag like `--system` with `uv pip install`. ([gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com/caoer/5b9bbd0fd9fb1dd20d6812b02cfdc3b7?utm_source=openai))\n\n3. Lock and sync dependencies with uv.\n   - Use `uv sync` (or `uv pip sync`) rather than ad-hoc pip installs. ([gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com/caoer/5b9bbd0fd9fb1dd20d6812b02cfdc3b7?utm_source=openai))  \n   - Commit `pyproject.toml` and `requirements.txt` (locked) files; never commit virtual environment directories. ([gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com/PierreVannier/316df92beba16cab68649e23103fbe39?utm_source=openai))\n\n4. {"contents":"---\ndescription: Rules for generating shell commands in terminal contexts\nglobs: *\n---\n\n## SHELL COMMAND GENERATION\n\nWhen generating shell commands that will be executed in a terminal:\n\n### AVOID EXCLAMATION POINTS IN STRINGS\n- **NEVER** use exclamation points (`!`) inside double-quoted strings in shell commands\n- Exclamation points trigger history expansion in zsh/bash and cause `dquote>` prompts\n- Instead of `echo \"Done!\"`, use `echo \"Done\"` or `echo 'Done!'` (single quotes)\n- Instead of `echo \"Success! All tests passed!\"`, use `echo \"Success. All tests passed.\"` or `echo 'Success! All tests passed!'`\n\n### EXAMPLES\n\nBad (causes dquote> prompt in zsh):\n```bash\necho \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue!\"\necho \"✅ All tests passed!\"\n```\n\nGood (works in all shells):\n```bash\necho \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue\"\necho \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue.\"\necho 'Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue!'\necho \"✅ All tests passed\"\nprintf '%s\\n' \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue!\"\n```\n\n### WHY THIS MATTERS\n- In zsh, `!` inside double quotes triggers history expansion\n- This causes the shell to wait for more input, showing `dquote>` prompt\n- Users must manually type `\"` to continue, breaking automation\n- Single quotes or avoiding `!` entirely prevents this issue\n\n### GENERAL BEST PRACTICES\n- Prefer single quotes for literal strings with special characters\n- Use `printf '%s\\n' \"...\"` for complex strings\n- Keep echo messages professional without unnecessary punctuation\n- Avoid emoji + exclamation combinations like `\"✅ Done!\"`\n","totalLinesInFile":44}

The info is current as of late 2025 / early 2026.  \n\n---\n\n## Key Rule Types & Locations\n\n| Rule Type | Where It’s Stored | Scope / Applies To | Typical Uses |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **Global / User Rules** | In the Cursor app’s settings: *Settings → General → Rules for AI*. These are plain text, global rules. ([learncursor.dev](https://learncursor.dev/features/rules?utm_source=openai)) | Applies to **all projects** you open in Cursor, regardless of their repo structure. Always included. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai)) | Setting consistent personal preferences: tone/style, always reply in English, output formatting, etc. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai)) |\n| **Project Rules** | In each project’s `.cursor/rules/` folder; the files inside are `.mdc` format, version-controlled with your repo. Subfolders can also have their own `.cursor/rules` so you can have nested/project-segment-specific rules. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai)) | Applies only when working in that project. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/context/rules?utm_source=openai)) | Project-specific conventions: code style, architecture decisions, domain-knowledge, automated workflows. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai)) |\n| **Legacy: `.cursorrules` file** | A single file in the project root, earlier approach. Still supported, but deprecated, in favor of `.cursor/rules/` folder structure. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai)) | Same project-scope usage, but less flexible compared to `.cursor/rules/`. Globally applied across project unless filtered inside file. ([cursordocs.com](https://cursordocs.com/en/docs/context/rules-for-ai?utm_source=openai)) | Migration path for older projects; simple guide-style rules you don’t need file-pattern control over. |\n\n---\n\n## How They Interact & Priority\n\n- **Global rules** are always loaded across Cursor sessions. They’re your top-level defaults. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai))  \n- **Project rules** can *override or add to* global rules (especially for project-specific issues). If a project rule says “use snake_case for service names in this project”, that’ll take precedence for files matching its glob. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai))  \n- The **legacy `.cursorrules`** still works, but new users are encouraged to migrate to the folder structure as it offers more clarity, multiple rule files, scoping by file types/globs, etc. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai))  \n\n---\n\n## Important Details, Known Issues & Best Practices\n\n- **File patterns / globbing**: Project rules can define globs (like `*.ts` or inside certain folder paths) so rules only apply to relevant files. Nested `.cursor/rules/` directories let you scope rules to specific subfolders. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/context/rules?utm_source=openai))  \n- **Automatic attachment / always apply**: Project rules have metadata like `alwaysApply`, or settings to auto-attach when certain files are referenced. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai))  \n- **Explicit invocation**: You can manually invoke a rule using `@ruleName` in chats/etc if the rule is marked “Manual” or “Agent Requested”. ([docs.cursor.com](https://docs.cursor.com/en/context/rules?utm_source=openai))  \n\n### Known Issues & User Frustrations\n\n- In **multi-project workspaces** (e.g. monorepos), rules in the workspace root or in one project sometimes take precedence or interfere when working in other projects. Cursor may mis-identify which project context it's in, resulting in odd behavior with rule application. ([forum.cursor.com](https://forum.cursor.com/t/cursor-rules-in-multi-project-workspaces/129557?utm_source=openai))  \n- Some users report **User/Global Rules** being ignored in favor of project rules or `.cursorrules`, or not reliably applied unless manually referenced. ([reddit.com](https://www.reddit.com//r/cursor/comments/1pwp9vt/my_user_rules_do_nothing_but_cursorrules_works/?utm_source=openai))  \n\n---\n\n## Summary & Recommendations\n\n- Use **Global/User Rules** for personal style / preferences that should apply everywhere.\n- Use **Project Rules** (`.cursor/rules` folder) to encode project-specific conventions and behaviours, especially when you need file-pattern control or need to version control them.\n- Rely on **`.cursorrules`** only if you’re dealing with older projects, or until you migrate to the newer folder structure. Wherever possible, you should move legacy rules into the project rules system.\n- If you have a **monorepo / multi-project workspace**, test carefully. Ensure your `.cursor/rules` directories are structured so Cursor can clearly resolve which rule applies where. You might run into priority/overlap conflicts otherwise.\n- Always version control your project rules so teammates share them and changes are tracked.\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can also pull up the exact metadata format for project-rule `.mdc` files (fields like `globs`, `alwaysApply`, etc.), examples, or how to migrate old `.cursorrules` files into the new structure."}],"isFinal":true,"rejected":false}

{"contents":"---\ndescription: Rules for generating shell commands in terminal contexts\nglobs: *\n---\n\n## SHELL COMMAND GENERATION\n\nWhen generating shell commands that will be executed in a terminal:\n\n### AVOID EXCLAMATION POINTS IN STRINGS\n- **NEVER** use exclamation points (`!`) inside double-quoted strings in shell commands\n- Exclamation points trigger history expansion in zsh/bash and cause `dquote>` prompts\n- Instead of `echo \"Done!\"`, use `echo \"Done\"` or `echo 'Done!'` (single quotes)\n- Instead of `echo \"Success! All tests passed!\"`, use `echo \"Success. All tests passed.\"` or `echo 'Success! All tests passed!'`\n\n### EXAMPLES\n\nBad (causes dquote> prompt in zsh):\n```bash\necho \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue!\"\necho \"✅ All tests passed!\"\n```\n\nGood (works in all shells):\n```bash\necho \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue\"\necho \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue.\"\necho 'Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue!'\necho \"✅ All tests passed\"\nprintf '%s\\n' \"Fixed CLIENT_DOMAIN redirect issue!\"\n```\n\n### WHY THIS MATTERS\n- In zsh, `!` inside double quotes triggers history expansion\n- This causes the shell to wait for more input, showing `dquote>` prompt\n- Users must manually type `\"` to continue, breaking automation\n- Single quotes or avoiding `!` entirely prevents this issue\n\n### GENERAL BEST PRACTICES\n- Prefer single quotes for literal strings with special characters\n- Use `printf '%s\\n' \"...\"` for complex strings\n- Keep echo messages professional without unnecessary punctuation\n- Avoid emoji + exclamation combinations like `\"✅ Done!\"`\n","totalLinesInFile":44}
